Incentives for self-employed people and employees. Self-employed workers are allowed to deduct VHI premiums from taxable income and employees are allowed to deduct employer-purchased VHI premiums from taxable income (up to a limit of €500 per covered person a year or €1500 per covered person with a disability). All insurance premiums are exempt from VAT. VHI premiums are also exempt from the insurance premium tax.

The basis for entitlement is residence and payment of contributions to the social health insurance (SHI) scheme. Anyone > 25, or < 25 and working or receiving social benefits, must register with a sickness fund and pay contributions in order to be covered. Coverage is automatically extended free of charge to dependent people > 25 and dependants with no income or a low income (less than €2950 in the first quarter of 2023). Income-related employee contributions are automatically deducted from gross wages. Self-employed people also pay contributions based on income. Some residents with no income or a low income (such as working students or self-employed people without work) are exempt from paying social contributions (for pensions, for example), but must pay a personal contribution directly to their sickness fund in order to have access to social health insurance benefits. The personal contribution is based on household income. In 2023 it ranged from €0 for people below the subsistence income level (that is, those eligible for the minimum income scheme) to a maximum of €881 per quarter [RIZIV-INAMI, 2023]. Homeless people can join a sickness fund if they register at a reference address such as a municipal welfare centre.

Entitlement is based on residence. In 2018 residence was re-established as the basis for entitlement to health services covered by the National Health System (NHS) and delivered by providers owned or contracted by the NHS at a regional level. Asylum seekers and refugees are entitled to the same benefits as residents. Undocumented migrants are also entitled to the same benefits as residents after being in Spain for 90 days or through a report from social services.

Refugees: same as residents.
Asylum seekers: entitled to some services. The law defines a list of services that are not covered or only partially covered by the social health insurance scheme but are covered for asylum seekers and a list of services that are not covered for asylum seekers [Dauvrin et al., 2019] [11].
Undocumented migrants: undocumented migrants can be covered by municipal welfare centres, which entitles them to emergency care (and, in principle, some preventive and curative care, including medicines) delivered in hospitals or in ambulatory settings. Welfare centres have discretion in the procedures and conditions they apply. Depending on their place of residence, undocumented migrants may have access to the same health care as residents or to a more limited set of services.

VHI does not usually fill gaps in population coverage. People from countries outside the European Union applying to stay for studies or temporary voluntary or other non-paid work or applying for long-term EU residence are required to buy VHI if they are not covered by any publicly financed scheme [Ministry of the Presidency, 2011] [1].
There are no waiting time guarantees or targets.

In 2011 the Ministry of Health used a royal decree (a type of law) to establish a legal framework for maximum waiting times for several surgical procedures (e.g. cardiac valve surgery, coronary surgery, cataracts and hip and knee replacement) [Ministry of Health, 2011] [9]. The regions translated the national rule into regional legislation, but the pace of implementation has varied, with some introducing waiting time guarantees before the national rule (in the early 2000s) and others not until 2018 (Asturias). Under the national rule, people must be offered an alternative public or private provider if the maximum waiting time is exceeded. Some regions also have maximum waiting times for outpatient specialist visits.

The social health insurance (SHI) scheme provides a single, national benefits package. However, services not covered by the SHI scheme may be covered by the mandatory complementary health insurance (CHI) provided by five of the six sickness funds, and these benefits can vary by sickness fund. The public fund does not provide mandatory CHI. People covered by the public fund can obtain mandatory CHI from the other sickness funds.

Mandatory CHI covers services like health promotion, orthodontics, optical care (glasses and contact lenses), osteopathy and chiropractic, as well as emergency medical assistance abroad and ambulance transport. Some sickness funds also cover co-payments for visits to general practitioners and specialists for children. Sickness funds can determine the content of the mandatory CHI coverage they offer and use this to try and attract new members. In the past decade, however, stricter regulation has aimed to harmonize mandatory CHI benefits. Also, as local sickness funds in the same national alliance have merged, the merged fund offers the same mandatory CHI benefits, which makes the market more transparent. In contrast to SHI benefits, mandatory CHI is financed through flat-rate contributions, which are regressive. Coverage is automatically extended to dependants free of charge.

The National Health System provides a single, national benefits package (the common package). Regions (known as Autonomous Communities) can provide additional benefits if they have the resources needed to finance them (the complementary package) [Ministry of the Presidency, 2012] [3]. In practice, regional variations are negligible. The trend is to extend the common package to meet changing population needs and to move towards even greater nation-wide uniformity.

According to official statistics, at least 1% of the population (about 115 000 people) is not covered by the social health insurance (SHI) scheme – mostly people who are not able to pay social contributions or are not aware of the administrative requirements [Devos & et al., 2019] [12] [RIZIV-INAMI, 2022] [23]. Self-employed people are also more likely to lack SHI coverage, partly due to the complexity of rules around enrolment [Cès & Baeten, 2020] [9]. The share of people not covered by the SHI scheme is slightly higher – at least 2% – in the Brussels region and among people aged between 25 and 40 years, which may in part reflect the higher prevalence of workers covered under international arrangements living and working in Brussels.

The actual share of the population that is not covered is higher than official statistics suggest, however, because the official statistics do not include undocumented migrants, prisoners or homeless people, who also lack SHI coverage [RIZIV-INAMI, 2014] [25].
Foreigners granted temporary residence for family reunification and undocumented migrants who have been in Spain for less than 90 days and who do not have a report from social services.

Heavy and complex co-payments are applied to almost all health services, including primary care visits.
There are very few exemptions from co-payments and no general exemption for people with low incomes.
Reduced co-payments are not automatically granted to low-income households and there are major gaps in take-up.
Balance billing is widespread in hospitals (‘fee supplements’) and also occurs in outpatient care.
Co-payment protection mechanisms do not apply to balance billing.
Most outpatient care is subject to retrospective reimbursement.

Percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products (ortho-prosthetic devices such as supportive braces and splints, prostheses, wheelchairs, crutches and hearing aids). Several protection mechanisms are in place – for example, a monthly cap on co-payments for pensioners and exemptions from co-payments for several groups of disadvantaged people, including some people with low incomes. However, there are no exemptions from co-payments for children or for many low-income households and there is no cap for non-pensioners. 

Access to protection mechanisms may be hindered by administrative barriers when there is an application process in place (for example, for beneficiaries of the minimum vital income scheme) or delayed until the beginning of the following year because the user database collecting data on income and working status is only updated once a year.
Social health insurance coverage of dental care, medical products and over-the-counter medicines is limited.

The National Health System (NHS) does not cover optical care for children or adults or hearing aids for people aged over 26. The range of dental services covered by the NHS is very limited for adults (tooth extraction and treatment of infections or inflammation only). Preventive dental services are only covered for children, pregnant women and people with dental issues caused by cancer treatment or congenital malformations.

Benefits in kind (third-party payment) only automatically apply to hospital-based care and outpatient medicines. Most outpatient care is subject to retrospective reimbursement rather than provided as a benefit in kind, which is highly unusual among health systems in high-income countries. Since 2015 general practitioners have been required to apply a third-party payment to people entitled to reduced co-payments (known as ‘increased reimbursement’ in Belgium). In January 2022 the right to apply a third-party payment to all patients was extended to all other outpatient health care providers on a voluntary basis.

The National Institute for Health and Disability Insurance (RIZIV-INAMI), which manages and supervises the mandatory social health insurance scheme, is responsible for defining user charges policy.

This type of policy is regulated by law or royal decree (another type of law) and must be approved by the Spanish parliament.

Reduced co-payments (referred to as ‘increased reimbursement’ in Belgium) are applied automatically for the following groups of eligible people only: people with a means-tested subsistence income (those eligible for the minimum income scheme, which benefited around 1.4% of the population – about 150 000 people – in January 2022); older people with a means-tested income guarantee (social assistance for older people); people with disabilities receiving a means-tested allowance; children with disabilities < 21; orphans; and unaccompanied foreign minors.

The following groups of eligible people need to request reduced co-payments: low-income households not in the automatic entitlement category. For applications in 2023, low-income households are those in which the household’s annual gross taxable income in 2022 is < €23 304, increased by €4314 for each additional household member.

Many people eligible for reduced co-payments do not benefit from any reduction. Data from 2012 suggest that around 480 000 eligible households did not apply for reduced co-payments [Farfan-Portet et al., 2019] [17]. Analysis finds that a third of people at risk of poverty in 2016 did not benefit from reduced co-payments [Bouckaert et al., 2020] [6]. Survey data from 2019–2020 indicate that non-take-up of reduced co-payments is nearly 70% in adults aged between 18 and 64 who are eligible based on low household income and nearly 40% in people aged over 65 [Goedemé et al., 2022] [19]. In response to this weakness, RIZIV-INAMI and the sickness funds have been more active in trying to identify and inform potential beneficiaries, working closely with the tax administration [RIZIV-INAMI, 2019] [21].

The annual cap on co-payments (maximum billing, MAF) is applied automatically. The fixed caps that apply to children or households entitled to reduced co-payments can be easily determined. The caps based on income also follow an automated procedure. Once a household has paid €250 in co-payments in a year, making it eligible for the lowest income-related cap), the net taxable income of the household in the previous two years is checked to determine whether the household is eligible for the lowest income-related cap [RIZIV-INAMI, 2021] [22]. Once a household has exceeded the appropriate cap, co-payments for outpatient medicines or inpatient care are no longer applied; co-payments in outpatient care continue to be applied but are then retrospectively reimbursed.

Yes. Mechanisms to protect people from co-payments for outpatient prescribed medicines (reduced co-payments, exemptions and caps) are applied automatically in pharmacies through the e-prescription system. The user database is only updated once a year, however. This means that residents who experience a change in status (e.g. become unemployed, earn less money, develop a relevant health condition) may have to wait for up to a year before benefiting from protection mechanisms.

Some people may not benefit from protection mechanisms due to administrative barriers. For example, people receiving the minimum vital income (Ingreso Mínimo Vital in Spanish) are exempt from co-payments but, as of December 2021, only 40% of eligible households were getting the income [AIReF, 2022] [16].

Anecdotal evidence suggests that waiting times for outpatient and inpatient care are reduced in return for accepting balance billing and, in rare cases, informal payments [Annemans, 2016] [1] [Belgische Kamer van volksvertegenwoordigers, 2017] [4] [Bertels, 2020] [5] [Weeghmans, 2018] [27].

Waiting times are not monitored.

Waiting times are a problem, particularly for specialist consultations and some surgical procedures, and have increased since 2010, when budgets began to be cut in response to the economic crisis following the global financial crisis of 2008.

The share of people waiting for more than two months for an outpatient visit has increased since 2011 [Oliva et al., 2018] [4]. Official data indicate that from 2006 to 2022, the average waiting time for a first consultation with a specialist and for non-urgent surgery rose from 54 to 95 days and from 70 to 120 days, respectively; and the number of people waiting for non-urgent surgery rose from 9.4 to 17.1 per 100 000 people [Ministry of Health, 2023a] [5]. Waiting times worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic due to mechanisms introduced to prioritize urgent and cancer surgery during the sharpest waves. Specific programs are now trying to reduce the backlog of pending surgeries and specialist consultations.

In 2022 only 23% of interviewees reported receiving attention in primary care within two days of asking for an appointment, down from 86% in 2016 [Ministry of Health, 2023b] [6].

The low availability of psychologists and psychiatrists and anecdotal evidence suggest that waiting times for psychological and psychiatric attention are a substantial barrier to accessing mental health services [Urbanos-Garrido et al., 2021] [7].

People covered by mutual funds (MUGEJU, MUFACE, ISFAS) who opt for provision through private providers are entitled to the services covered by the National Health System but benefit from shorter waiting times. People with chronic conditions or those who are more likely to require complex surgery are less likely to opt for private provision and thus more likely to experience long waiting times for publicly provided care [González López-Valcárcel & Pinilla Domínguez, 2022] [8].

VHI offered by sickness funds through mutual health insurance companies are regulated by the Control Service of Health Insurance Funds; VHI offered by private for-profit companies is regulated by the Financial Services and Markets Authority (FSMA).

Heavy and complex co-payments are applied to almost all health services, including primary care visits.

There are very few exemptions from co-payments and no general exemption for people with low incomes.

Reduced co-payments are not automatically granted to low-income households and there are major gaps in take-up.

Balance billing is widespread in hospitals (‘fee supplements’) and also occurs in outpatient care.

Co-payment protection mechanisms do not apply to balance billing.

Most outpatient care is subject to retrospective reimbursement.

Percentage co-payments are applied to outpatient prescribed medicines and medical products (ortho-prosthetic devices such as supportive braces and splints, prostheses, wheelchairs, crutches and hearing aids). Several protection mechanisms are in place – for example, a monthly cap on co-payments for pensioners and exemptions from co-payments for several groups of disadvantaged people, including some people with low incomes. However, there are no exemptions from co-payments for children or for many low-income households and there is no cap for non-pensioners.

Access to protection mechanisms may be hindered by administrative barriers when there is an application process in place (for example, for beneficiaries of the minimum vital income scheme) or delayed until the beginning of the following year because the user database collecting data on income and working status is only updated once a year.

The National Institute for Health and Disability Insurance (RIZIV-INAMI) manages and supervises the mandatory social health insurance (SHI) scheme. It is responsible for the national fee schedule (the so-called “nomenclature”), sets tariffs for health services (including medicines) and defines user charges policy.

All SHI benefits except outpatient medicines, hospital stays and lump sums for specific conditions (such as incontinence, people in need of palliative care, people in a vegetative state) are listed in the nomenclature, which defines tariffs and user charges. The nomenclature is determined by Royal Decree and is updated regularly. It contains more than 15 000 codes.

The Commission for the Reimbursement of Pharmaceuticals, part of RIZIV-INAMI, decides on coverage of outpatient and inpatient medicines. It involves physicians, pharmacists, universities, sickness funds (who have voting rights), the pharmaceutical industry, the ministers of social affairs, public health, economic affairs and finance and RIZIV-INAMI (who does not have voting rights). Decisions are based on five evaluative criteria: therapeutic value, price and the proposed basis for coverage, therapeutic and social importance, budget impact for the SHI scheme and cost-effectiveness (but cost-effectiveness analysis is only required when a product claims to have added therapeutic value) [Gerkens & Merkur, 2020] [18].

Coverage of medical products includes implants or invasive medical devices on a positive list and non-implantable devices such as hearing aids, glasses and contact lenses for people with certain medical conditions. Criteria for coverage include therapeutic and social importance, budgetary impact and cost-effectiveness. As a result, coverage of hearing aids and optical care (glasses and contact lenses) is limited to products and covered people that meet the criteria.

Items excluded from the nomenclature are typically not covered by the SHI scheme – for example, alternative therapies such as acupuncture, homoeopathy and osteopathy. However, these therapies may be partially covered by the mandatory complementary health insurance (CHI) provided by five of the six sickness funds (all except the public fund). People covered by the public fund can obtain mandatory CHI from the other funds.

Coverage policy is governed centrally by the national Ministry of Health and the highest governing body of the National Health System (NHS) – the Interterritorial Council – a collegiate governance body comprising the 17 regional health ministers and the national Minister of Health.

The definition of the benefits package (common and complementary) and the methods used to change it are regulated by a royal decree (Ministry of Health, 2006) [2], which is regularly updated.

The Interterritorial Council defines the common package based on proposals submitted by the Commission on Benefits, Insurance and Financing and technical advice from the Spanish Network of Agencies for Health Technology Assessment and Benefits. This Network develops an annual joint program of health technology assessment reports and provides advice on the inclusion or exclusion of health technologies before any decision is made by the Interterritorial Council.

Each region (Autonomous Community) can define an additional complementary package if they have the resources needed to finance them and can meet three further conditions: justification for the need; allocation of sufficient financial resources to the common package; and adherence to the budgetary stability criteria established by the national Ministry of Finance. In practice, regional variation in publicly financed services is negligible.

For medicines and medical products, the Spanish Agency for Medicines and Medical Products (AEMPS in Spanish) is responsible for market authorization of medicines and medical products approved by the European Medicines Agency. Pricing and coverage decisions are carried out by the Ministry of Health’s Commission on Benefits, Insurance and Financing and the Interministerial Commission for Medicine Pricing (CIPM in Spanish) based on therapeutic reports (Informes de Posicionamiento Terapéutico in Spanish). These reports were introduced in 2013 and are the reference instrument for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of medicines in the NHS. In 2020 the Ministry of Health approved a “Plan for the consolidation of therapeutic reports in the NHS”, which aims to improve the prioritization, follow up and governance of the reports.

Reduced co-payments: yes, for people eligible for ‘increased reimbursement’ (mainly people with a low income, disabled children and orphans).
Exemptions from co-payments: yes, for children < 18 for dental care and people registered with community health services for outpatient care (general practice, nursing, physiotherapy).
Cap on co-payments: yes, an annual cap on co-payments (known as ‘maximum billing’, MAF) based on income, age or health status
VHI covers co-payments: yes, it partly covers balance billing and co-payments but mainly focuses on (but is not limited to) inpatient care and dental care

Reduced user charges: lower percentage co-payments based on income and also for most medicines for chronic conditions (46% of covered medicines in 2021) [Ministry of Health, 2022a] [14].

Exemption from user charges: yes, on the basis of income, health status and other criteria. In 2022 16% of the population (7.5 million people) were exempt from co-payments [Ministry of Health, 2022b] [15].

Cap on user charges: yes, for pensioners on the basis of income. In 2022 15% of the population (6.9 million people) were protected by the cap [Ministry of Health, 2022b] [15].

VHI covers user charges: no.

Workforce shortages in the following areas increasingly cause access problems: nursing staff in all sectors, general practitioners (GP) and dentists who no longer accept new patients (almost 20% of GPs), some medical specialists (for example, geriatricians) [Beersmans et al., 2023] [3].

Administrative barriers can limit access to the National Health System for people who experience a change in financial circumstances and must wait for the new tax year to benefit from protection from user charges (co-payments); undocumented migrants (legal loopholes and delays in getting social services to authorize access); foreigners legally reunited with relatives in Spain; asylum seekers (delays in the process of being recognized as an asylum seeker); and people wanting to be treated outside their region.

Reliable data on the share of the population with VHI are not available. It is estimated that there were 10.2 million VHI policies in 2020 (58% in commercial insurers and 42% in sickness funds) in a population of 11.6 million people. This is likely to include a significant amount of double counting, however, as individuals can be covered through multiple policies [Assuralia, 2023] [2] [Controledienst voor de ziekenfondsen, 2022] [10] [Van de Voorde et al., 2011] [26].

Supplementary VHI providing faster access to treatment: 20.8% in 2021, up from 16.7% in 2016 [IDIS, 2022] [11]. This figure does not include the 1.7 million civil servants and their dependents (covered by mutual funds: MUFACE, MUGEJU and ISFAS) who opt to use health services delivered by private providers.

Complementary VHI (services) covering dental care: around 11% (2020), a significant increase from 8% in 2015 [UNESPA, 2021] [12].

Note that a person can obtain both types of VHI through a single policy.

The share of the population with VHI varies widely across regions; Madrid, Catalonia and the Balearic Islands have the highest rates of VHI coverage [UNESPA, 2022] [13].

People need some form of ID to access health services. Asylum seekers (when consulting outside the reception network) and undocumented migrants also need a “guarantee of payer” from FEDASIL (the federal agency for the reception of asylum seekers) or the municipal welfare centre. Undocumented migrants need to have an official address. Asylum seekers need to be registered as asylum applicants; those with a work permit are eligible to be covered by the social health insurance (SHI) scheme. The extent to which asylum seekers face special administrative requirements depends on their place of stay and the nature of the health care they need (e.g. specialist care). Unaccompanied minors (whether they apply for asylum or not) are eligible to be covered by the SHI scheme if they have a mentor recognized by the Ministry of Justice.
People need a health card to access all health services except emergency care and maternal and child health care.

A 2022 Special Eurobarometer report on corruption finds that 3% of survey respondents in Belgium who had visited a health care practitioner or institution in the previous 12 months reported having had to make an extra payment or give a valuable gift to a nurse or doctor or make a donation to the hospital on top of the official fees [European Commission, 2022] [16]. This is in line with the EU15 average of 3% and a decrease compared to the previous assessment (6% in 2020, 5% in 2017, 2% in 2014) [European Commission, 2014] [13] [European Commission, 2017] [14] [European Commission, 2020] [15]. It is possible that some people may mistake balance billing for an informal payment, perhaps due to a lack of information or uncertainty about whether balance billing will be charged, how much it will cost and whether it will be covered by VHI.

Informal payments are not an issue. Eurobarometer surveys consistently find Spain to have one of the lowest levels of self-reported informal payments in the European Union [European Commission, 2022] [10].
The Minister of Public Health and Social Affairs is responsible for defining population coverage.

Access to specialist outpatient care does not require a general practitioner (GP) referral. People can ask a GP to manage their medical information through a global medical record, which improves coordination among health care providers. The global medical record system was introduced in 2001 and the share of covered people benefiting from it has increased from 32% in 2003 to 81% in 2020 [IMA-AIM, 2023] [20].

Access to covered medicines usually requires a prescription, but some covered medicines (e.g. painkillers) can also be obtained without a prescription, but at a higher price.

Most outpatient care is subject to retrospective reimbursement rather than provided as a benefit in kind.

User charges are applied to most health services, including medicines. The design of user charges policy is highly complex, involving co-payments, multiple mechanisms to protect people from co-payments and widespread balance billing. There is no cap on the volume of covered health services.

Access to non-emergency care requires registration with a primary care centre. Publicly financed health services are provided by a mix of public and private providers contracted by the National Health System (NHS). Access to covered specialist care (outpatient and inpatient) requires a referral from family doctors. Access to covered medicines requires a prescription. There is no retrospective reimbursement; all benefits are provided in kind. User charges (co-payments) are applied to outpatient medicines and medical products. There is no cap on the volume of covered health services.

Some civil servants in the central administration, members of the armed forces and members of the judiciary (1.7 million people) are covered by the Mutual Fund for State Civil Servants (MUFACE), the Social Institute for the Armed Forces (ISFAS) and the General Justice Mutual Fund (MUGEJU), respectively. They can choose to have their care delivered by the National Health System or by private providers contracted by the mutual funds. Those who opt for provision through private providers have direct access (without referral) to specialist care and may benefit from faster access to treatment.
VHI covering dental care is available but take-up is limited.

20.8% of the population had VHI offering faster access to outpatient specialist care, inpatient care and diagnostic tests in 2021 [IDIS, 2022] [11]; around 11% had VHI covering dental care in 2020 [UNESPA, 2021] [12]. The share of the population with VHI varies widely across regions; Madrid, Catalonia and the Balearic Islands have the highest rates of VHI coverage [UNESPA, 2022] [13].

VHI (offered by sickness funds and private for-profit companies): there is open enrolment and lifetime coverage. They cannot refuse to cover high-risk people, but they can exclude costs linked to (for example) pre-existing conditions. If a person takes out VHI with a sickness fund they must choose the same sickness fund that provides them with social health insurance coverage.

Since 2007, private for-profit companies have only been able to change the premiums and benefits of individual policies in specific cases such as an adjustment linked to changes in the health index [Gerkens & Merkur, 2020] [18].

People not covered by the social health insurance (SHI) scheme are entitled to emergency care and some preventive services, such as vaccinations for children, which are free at the point of use and co-financed by the federal government and the federated entities. Only people covered by the SHI scheme have free access to preventive services such as breast cancer screening.

Undocumented migrants can be covered by municipal welfare centres, which entitles them to emergency care (and, in principle, some preventive and curative care, including medicines) delivered in hospitals or in ambulatory settings. Welfare centres have discretion in the procedures and conditions they apply. Depending on their place of residence, undocumented migrants may have access to the same health care as residents or to a more limited set of services.

Prisoners are currently covered by the Ministry of Justice, but steps have been taken to integrate their coverage with the SHI scheme from January 2023 at the earliest.

Homeless people can join a sickness fund if they register at a reference address such as a municipal welfare centre.
